title: Burst efficiency and cold-start penalty vs batching — one-pager (Apr 2026)
body:
Purpose:
This note captures a compact set of benchmarking observations about how short bursts interact with batching, model quantization, and cold-start penalties. Audience: SRE, serving-runtime, and product folks deciding default batching and prewarm heuristics for bursty workloads (webchat, search assistant hits).

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- Small bursts (1–10 concurrent requests) are dominated by cold-start overhead when instances are not prewarmed; batching helps, but only when requests can be coalesced within the warmup window.
- Aggressive quantization (int8) reduces per-token cost but increases cold-start wall-time by ~10–18% vs fp16 on our kernel selection path; for ultra-low-latency bursts this tradeoff can be worse than the steady-state savings.
- For workloads with median request size ~120 tokens and burstiness index > 2, targetting a short prewarm pool (1–2 GPUs per shard) with opportunistic batching (window=30ms) gives the best burst efficiency / cost balance in our tests.

Experiment setup (short):
- Model variants: 1) base-7B fp16, 2) base-7B int8-quant.
- Hardware: single A100-40GB equivalent (cloud reserved pool) for all runs.
- Workload: Poisson arrivals tuned for three burst shapes: microburst (50 rps for 200ms), short burst (10 rps for 2s), sustained (5 rps for 30s).
- Measurement windows: cold (container and model not resident; spin-up includes kernel selection + weight load), warm (hot KV cache, model resident).
- Batching: immediate (batch=1), small-window (30ms), medium-window (100ms).
- Metrics: P50 / P95 latency (ms) observed at client, tokens/sec effective throughput, dollars per 1k tokens (rough unit cost using internal costing).

Representative results (median of 5 runs each) — textual table:

Scenario                   | Batch    | Variant  | Cold P95 (ms) | Warm P95 (ms) | P50 (ms) | Cost /1k tok (USD)
---------------------------|----------|----------|---------------|---------------|----------|------------------
Microburst (50rps,200ms)   | 1        | fp16     | 950           | 260           | 140      | 0.92             
Microburst                 | 30ms     | fp16     | 880           | 210           | 120      | 0.78             
Microburst                 | 30ms     | int8     | 1040          | 240           | 130      | 0.63             
Short burst (10rps,2s)     | 1        | fp16     | 820           | 180           | 100      | 0.95             
Short burst                | 100ms    | fp16     | 760           | 150           | 95       | 0.82             
Short burst                | 30ms     | int8     | 880           | 170           | 98       | 0.60             
Sustained (5rps,30s)       | 1        | fp16     | 810           | 120           | 85       | 0.99             
Sustained                  | 100ms    | int8     | 920           | 110           | 80       | 0.58             

Notes on table: 'Cold P95' includes container spin + weight load + kernel selection. Warm numbers assume model hot and kv-cache primed. Cost /1k tok is internal blended cost (compute + amortized infra).

Textual chart: relative burst-efficiency heatmap (rows: batch window, cols: scenario; value = warm P95 / cost per 1k tokens) — higher is better (efficiency):

Values: (rounded)
- immediate: microburst 284, short 189, sustained 121
- 30ms window: microburst 269, short 183, sustained (N/A for sustained as batching larger)
- 100ms window: microburst 271, short 183, sustained 134

Interpretation: Costs drop sharply with quantization in steady-state, but cold P95 for int8 is consistently higher because load+kernel path picks a compatibility mode (we still see a ~10–18% extra latency until we stabilize). Batching windows >30ms provide diminishing returns for microbursts (they miss a lot of incoming packets), but help significantly for short bursts and sustained flows.

Key operational takeaways (practical):
- For web-facing bursty workloads where 95th ms matters, enable a short resident prewarm pool scaled to expected peak RPS in the 100–500ms window. Prewarm sizing heuristic: target 50–60% of peak concurrent requests so KV-cache hit helps.
- Default per-model quantization policy: prefer int8 for reserved/dedicated nodes with steady traffic; keep fp16 as default for on-demand/shared pools that see frequent cold cycles.
- Batching policy: opportunistic window=30ms as a conservative default for hosted API; allow customer-configurable windows up to 100ms for high-throughput users.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What is the library/kernel cause of the int8 cold penalty? (next: trace the weight load paths and kernel selection logs during spin-up — INF-973).
- Can we pre-stage kernel selection outcomes in a tiny cache to avoid re-probing on container start? (proto task in serving-runtime: #4821).
- Quantify real customer impact: map our synthetic burst shapes to top-10 PLG apps (telemetry + analytics) and compute expected lost SLA windows.

Quick action items:
- (eng-serving-runtime) Add a startup tracepoint that dumps kernel-selection time and quantization branch at instance init — owner: Diego Morales — ETA: 2w.
- (observability) Create a dashboard that overlays cold-spin incidents with customer 95th latency spikes — owner: Lin Zhao — ETA: 1w.
- (product) Draft default policy: int8 recommended for dedicated clusters, fp16 for shared-hosted — owner: Priya Nandakumar — ETA: 3w.

Appendix: quick handwritten style notes (raw):
- Microburst behaviour surprising: batching window too long -> misses the burst. For 50rps/200ms bursts batching needs <20ms to capture >30% coalescence. Our platform's socket aggregation adds ~8ms jitter.
- Cost math back-of-envelope: int8 reduces per-token kernel ops by ~28% -> compute cost down from 0.94 to ~0.64 USD/1k in these runs. But cold penalty can add 120–250ms which kills user experience for chat.
- UX tradeoffs: some customers prefer deterministic P95 over lower average cost. We should make conservative defaults and expose knobs.

If you want, I can convert the table into a simple CSV and push to the shared metrics bucket, or run a follow-up sweep that varies token length (50, 120, 400) to show scale effects.

Unresolved: should we consider a 'transient prewarm' that keeps kernels hot but swaps weights lazily? (sketch: keep a tiny shim process that holds kernel selection state — pros/cons TBD).

End of note.
